item.research_question: Can electrodeposition be used to simultaneously achieve nanometer-scale crystal grain refinement and fabricate thick (macroscopic) FeCoNi medium-entropy alloys to enable precise tensile testing?
item.material_system: Equiatomic FeCoNi medium-entropy alloys (specifically Fe34Co31Ni35, Fe34Co29Ni35, and Fe32Co33Ni34)
item.processing_route: Electrodeposition in an aqueous solution containing boric acid, hydroxylammonium chloride, saccharin sodium dihydrate, sodium dodecyl sulfate, nickel(II) sulfamate tetrahydrate, cobalt(II) sulfate heptahydrate, and iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate; solution temperature 55 ± 4 °C; cathode current density 50 mA cm−2; duration ~50 h per sample; copper substrates used as cathode.
item.test_conditions: Tensile testing at a strain rate of 1.0 × 10−3 s−1 and 20 °C; Vickers hardness testing with a 100 gf load at 10 s and 20 °C; annealing at 500–800 °C for 1 h for grain size variation; XRD and TEM characterization.
key_findings: Fabricated 0.2-mm thick equiatomic FeCoNi MEAs with a crystallite size of ~10 nm.
Sample C exhibited the highest ultimate tensile stress (UTS) of 1.6 GPa.
Samples A, B, and C showed fracture elongations of 1.4%, 1.6%, and 3.3%, respectively.
Vickers hardness values were consistent across samples: 506 HV, 497 HV, and 513 HV.
The 200 orientation index varied among samples (0.18, 0.13, and 0.25) and correlated with ductility.
Hardness vs. grain size data for grains >0.5 μm followed the Hall-Petch relation: HV = 131.1d−1/2 + 97.3.
As-deposited samples with ~10 nm grains exhibited higher hardness than annealed samples with ~0.5 μm grains but lower strengthening than extrapolated from the Hall-Petch relation.
The 1.6 GPa tensile strength is the highest reported UTS for a FeCoNi MEA.
item.mechanism: The lower strengthening observed at ~10 nm grain size compared to the extrapolated Hall-Petch relationship indicates the onset of the inverse Hall-Petch effect, where grain boundary deformation (sliding, migration, rotation) becomes dominant over dislocation movement in the grain interior, causing the conventional strengthening mechanisms to stop working.
item.limitations: Controlling grain size via heat treatment is difficult due to abnormal grain growth causing leaps from nanometer to micrometer order; the exact reason for crystal orientation changes between samples is not clear; the conventional model of HEAs/MEAs may not apply to deformation behaviors in nanocrystalline regimes.
item.future_work: Further development of the fabrication process is needed to clarify the effects of alloying elements on the deformation of nanocrystalline HEAs/MEAs; the dependence of strength on grain size near the peak should be detailed by controlling grain size via electrodeposition parameters such as additive agents and current density.
quotes: The nanocrystalline FeCoNi MEAs exhibit the maximum tensile strength of 1.6 GPa, which is the highest reported result to date.
The ductility of the samples depends on the 200 orientation index, the same way as in electrodeposited nickel.
